Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (in short the 'PFA Act') and further sentenced to imprisonment uptill the rising of the Court and pay fine of Rs. 500/- under Section 16(1)(a)(ii) of the PFA Act.
.
Both the sentences shall run concurrently.

2. Brief facts of the case are that on 19.6.1995 T.S.Verma, Food Inspector, Kangra visited the Karyana shop of accused at around 2:30 p.m. situated at village Nangal Chowk and found that accused had stocked 10 kilograms of Haldi of Powder for sale to the general public.
After serving notice of his intention to purchase the sample of Haldi powder on the rt accused, the Food Inspector purchased 600 Gms of Haldi powder from the accused against payment.
Thereafter the said sample was divided into three equal parts and was put in dry and clean polythene bags which were made air tight and after labeling were wrapped in accordance with rules.
Panchnama of the proceedings was also prepared which was witnessed by Shankar Dass and Ramesh Chand.
Thereafter one part of the same was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis while remaining two parts were deposited in the office of LHA, Kangra in accordance with rules.

Report dated 28.7.1995 of the Public Analyst declared the sample as adulterated, as the contents of the sample contained maize starch and un-permitted yellow oil soluble coal tar dye as an admixture, whereas Haldi powder should be free from foreign substances and added colouring matter.
Food Analyst further observed that sale of powdered spices except under packed condition is prohibited under the provisions of Rule 49 (24) of the PFA Act.
After receipt of the report of Food Analyst, the Food Inspector obtained the written consent from Chief Medical .
Officer, Kangra and thereafter prosecution was launched against the accused.
As sufficient grounds were found against accused, he was accordingly summoned and thereafter complainant record pre-charge evidence.

As a prima-facie case was found against the accused under the provisions of Food Adulteration of Act read with Rules framed thereunder, charges were framed against him, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

3. rt On the basis of material produced on record by the prosecution, the learned trial court held that the prosecution had proved the guilt of the accused for commission of offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Food and Adulteration Act and accordingly the accused was convicted and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for six months and pay fine of Rs. 1000/-
under the PFA Act.

4. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgment passed by the learned trial court, accused preferred an appeal before the learned appellate court and the learned appellate court dismissed the appeal filed by the accused and upheld the judgment of conviction passed by the learned trial court.
5. Feeling aggrieved by the said two judgments passed by the learned courts below, the accused has preferred the present revision petition.

sentences.text: 6. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and also gone through the records of the case.

7. In the present case, the accused has been convicted .
for commission of offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a) (i) and (ii) of the PFA Act.
Section 16 (1) (a)(i) and (ii) provides as under:-

"16. Penalties.- (1) Subject to the provisions of sub -section (1- A), if any person,-
(a) whether by himself or by any other person on of his behalf, imports into India or manufactures for sale, or stores, sells or distributes any article of food - (i) which is adulterated within the meaning of rt sub-clause (m) of Cl. (i-a) of Sec. 2 or misbranded within the meaning of Cl.(ix) of that section or the sale of which is prohibited under any provision of this Act or any rule made thereunder or by an order of the Food (Health) Authority;
(ii) other than an article of food referred to in sub-section (i) in contravention of any of the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder."
8.

As per the findings returned by the learned trial court, the accused in his statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. admitted that he had stocked 10 Kgs haldi powder for sale to the general public.

9. Rule 49 (24) of the PFA Rules 1955 provides as under:-
"(24) No person shall set powdered spices and condiments except under packed conditions."
10.
Under Rule 49(24) of the PFA Rules, no person can sell powdered spices and condiments except under packed conditions.
The case of the prosecution to the effect that the accused stocked Haldi power for sale to the general public in a gunny bag, was in contravention of abovementioned Rule stands .
duly proved on record.

Therefore, the findings returned by the learned trial court and affirmed by the learned appellate court to the effect that the sale of Haldi powder by the accused to general public in a gunny bag was in contravention of the provisions of Rule 49(24) of PFA Rules, 1955 cannot be faulted of with.
11. Similarly, it has been held by the learned trial court rt that the sample of Haldi powder purchased by the food inspector from the accused person is adulterated.

The report of the public analyst is on record as Ext. PJ, the relevant portion of the same reads as under: -

"I further certify that I have/had caused to be analysed the aforementioned sample and declare the result of the analysis to be as follows:-
1. Description -: the contents of the sample received in a polythene package packed by the food inspector.

(2) Physical examination Free from insects and mould growth(3)
Rodent hair and excreta-Absent(4) Moisture=8.91%(5) Total ash 4.14% (6) Ash insoluble in dilute HC1=1.45%

(7)Test for lead chromate=Negative 8.
Added artificial colouring matter=Unpermitted yellow oil soluble coal tar dye detected(9)
Microscopic examination:-
Maize starch structure seen alongwith haldi structure (10) total starch=50.71% and am of the opinion that the contents of the sample contain maize starch and unpermitted yellow oil solub le coal tar dye as an admixture, whereas haldi powder should be free from foreign substances and added colouring matter.
Use of unpermitted colouring matter in an article of food is not safe for human consumption.
The sample of haldi powder is, therefore, adulterated.

Moreover the sale of powdered spices except under packed conditions is prohibited under the provision of Rule 49(24) of PFA Rules".
12.

The contention of the defence that the food inspector had not properly taken the sample of haldi has been disbelieved by both the learned courts below and rightly so as it .
stands duly substantiated by the prosecution that the sample was drown properly.

A perusal of the report of public analyst demonstrates that the maize starch present in the sample of haldi has been found to the extent of 50.71% meaning thereby that more than half of the portion of the contents of the sample of of haldi taken by the food inspector was found to be that of maize starch.

The justification given by the defence that the rt maize starch was found because the food inspector used the same 'bhapka' and the scale which was used for selling maize flour to the customers is not convincing even if the contention of the defence is believed to be correct because even then presence of more than 50% of maize starch in the sample cannot be attributed to the alleged unclean bhapka and the scale.
Thus presence of more than 50% of maize starch in the haldi sample categorically demonstrates that the sample was adulterated.
Perusal of the judgment passed by the learned courts below demonstrates that all these aspects have been taken into consideration by the learned trial court as well as by the learned appellate court.

The learned trial court on the basis of the testimony of the prosecution witnesses and as well as on the basis of the appreciation of documentary evidence placed on record including the report by the public analyst has concluded that the accused had committed offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a) (i) and (ii) of the PFA Act.

The learned appellate court has also upheld the findings so returned by the learned .
trial court by giving a reasoned judgment in which the contention raised by the appellant have been duly taken into consideration alongwith the material placed on record by the prosecution and Ramesh Chand vs State Of H.P on 4 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/17296293/

sentences.text: 13. Further keeping in view the fact that neither it can be of said that the findings returned by the learned courts below are perverse or not borne out as per the record of the case, no case rt for in terference in its revisional jurisdiction has been made out by the present petitioner.
It is well settled law that the jurisdiction of High Court in revision is severely restricted and it cannot embark upon re -appreciation of evidence.

The High Court in revision cannot in absence of error on a point of law,
re- appreciate evidence and reverse a finding of law.

14. It has been further held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Janta Dal Vs. H.S. Chowdhury &
others, 1992 (4) SCC 305 that the object of the revis ional jurisdiction was to confer power upon superior criminal Courts a kind of paternal or supervisory jurisdiction in order to correct miscarriage of justice arising from misconception of law, irregularity of procedure, neglect of proper precaution or apparent harshness of treatment which has resulted on the one hand, or on the other hand in some undeserved hardship to individuals.

15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ram Briksh Singh and others Vs. Ambika Yadav and another,
(2004) 7 Supreme Court Cases 665, has again held that Revisional Court can interfere .
with the findings of lower court where the Courts below have overlooked material evidence.
16.

(2004) 7 Supreme Court Cases 665
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus it can be safely inferred that this Court has to exercise its revisional powers sparingly.
Though, this Court is not required to act as a Court of appeal, however, at the same time of it is the duty of the Court to correct manifest illegality resulting in gross miscarriage of justice.
However, I do not find any manifest rt illegality with the judgment passed by the learned courts below in the present case.

In view of the above discussion, I am of the considered view there is neither any perversity nor any infirmity with the judgments passed by the learned Courts below and the findings returned by the said Courts are duly substantiated from the records of the case.
In this view of the matter, the present revision petition is dismissed being devoid of any merit.
